nodes.label: Single-page scaffold
nodes.one_line: Generate a static HTML/CSS/JS page from a prompt and get it rendering correctly in a browser on the first or second pass.
know_what: Static site — HTML/CSS/JS served with no build step or server-side logic, the smallest unit an AI can scaffold end to end
Semantic HTML — using <nav>, <main>, <button> instead of generic <div>s so the AI's markup is accessible and inspectable by default
Single-file vs multi-file scaffold — one HTML file with inline <style>/<script> for a throwaway prompt, split files once the page is meant to last
CDN-linked libraries — pulling in a framework or icon set via a <script src> tag without a package manager, the fastest path from prompt to a running page
View-source verification — opening the rendered page's dev tools to confirm the DOM the AI claims it produced actually matches what loaded
Prompt-to-preview loop — the tool's built-in live preview (v0, Claude Artifacts, a local dev server) that shows the page without a manual copy-paste step
Placeholder content — Lorem ipsum, stock image URLs, and dummy links an AI inserts by default, which must be swapped before the page is real
know_how: State the page's purpose, sections, and any hard content in one prompt so the assistant doesn't guess at structure
Open the generated page immediately in a real browser, not just trust a description of what it does
Resize the viewport (mobile, tablet, desktop) before accepting the scaffold as done
Check every link and button actually does something instead of being a dead href
Ask for one revision at a time (change the hero, then the footer) instead of one giant re-prompt that regenerates the whole page
Diff the new HTML against the previous version to see exactly what changed on a revision
habits: Never accept a page as done from the chat transcript alone — always render it
Click every interactive element by hand before moving on
Keep the first working version saved before asking for the next revision
State constraints (no external fonts, no tracking scripts) up front instead of stripping them out after
Treat placeholder content as a checklist item, not a detail to forget
nodes.checkpoint: Given a one-paragraph description of a landing page (hero, three feature blocks, footer with links), produce a working HTML/CSS/JS page that renders correctly and has no dead links, in two prompts or fewer.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting the page because it 'looks right' in the chat transcript's description, without opening it in a browser — broken CSS, non-functional buttons, and layout overflow only show up on render, never in the code the assistant printed.

nodes.label: Component extraction
nodes.one_line: Ask an assistant to split a monolithic page into reusable components without changing what the page does.
know_what: Component — a self-contained chunk of markup, style, and behavior with a name and a boundary, the unit an AI needs to reason about one piece at a time
Props — the values a component takes as input instead of hardcoding content, what turns a one-off block into something reusable
Duplication signal — the same markup pattern appearing three or more times in a page, the concrete trigger for asking for extraction
Prop drilling — passing a value through several component layers that don't use it themselves, a smell an extraction can introduce if done carelessly
Naming by role, not appearance — calling a piece PricingCard instead of BlueBox, so future prompts can reference it by name
Behavior parity — the requirement that extraction changes structure, not output; the rendered page must look and act identical before and after
know_how: Point at the repeated markup and name the component you want extracted instead of asking for 'cleanup' in the abstract
Ask the assistant to list every prop a new component needs before it writes the component
Compare a screenshot or the rendered DOM before and after extraction to confirm nothing shifted
Extract one component per prompt so a bad extraction is easy to isolate and revert
Search the codebase afterward for any remaining copy of the pattern the extraction was meant to replace
Reject an extraction that changes visual output, even if the component 'looks cleaner' internally
habits: Before asking for a component, name what varies between its instances (the props) and what stays fixed
Read the extracted component's file in full, not just the diff summary, before accepting
Keep a component's file focused on one concern; push a second responsibility back to the assistant as a separate ask
Re-render the page after every extraction, not just after the whole pass is done
Flag any extraction that silently renamed a CSS class or id something else on the page depends on
nodes.checkpoint: Given a 200-line single-file page with a repeated card pattern, extract it into a parameterized component used by every instance, with the rendered page pixel-identical to before.
nodes.common_failure: Asking for a vague 'refactor into components' pass, which an assistant will happily do by inventing component boundaries that don't match how the page is actually reused — producing components with one caller each, or one god-component that just moved the mess.

nodes.label: Framework adoption
nodes.one_line: Move a static page into a framework (React, Vue, Svelte) with AI generating correct component boilerplate, checked spec-first and diff-by-diff.
know_what: Framework migration surface — every place a page's plain JS/DOM manipulation must become framework idioms (state, effects, event handlers)
Scaffolding tool — Vite, or a framework's own CLI, which lays out the project structure an AI should follow rather than invent
File-per-component convention — the framework's expected layout (one component per file, colocated styles), which an AI will violate if not told to follow it
Build step — the compile/bundle stage a framework introduces, meaning 'open in browser' now requires a dev server, not a double-click on the HTML file
Routing — client-side navigation (React Router, Vue Router, or a meta-framework's file-based router) replacing plain multi-page HTML links
Migration order — moving structure first, then styling, then behavior, so each AI pass has a narrow, checkable diff instead of one giant rewrite
Framework escape hatch — the ability to drop to raw DOM/CSS when the framework's abstraction doesn't fit, which an AI will avoid using unless prompted to consider it
know_how: Write the spec for the migration (which pages, which components, what stays out of scope) before the first migration prompt
Scaffold the framework project with its own CLI first, then ask the assistant to migrate content into that structure — never ask it to invent the project layout
Migrate one page or one component tree per session, verified and committed, before starting the next
Read every diff in the migration for accidental logic changes disguised as syntax translation
Run the dev server after each migrated piece, not just at the end of the whole migration
Ask explicitly whether the framework's idiomatic pattern (e.g. controlled inputs) was used, since an AI defaults to the plainest translation otherwise
habits: Treat 'migrate the whole app' as an instruction to refuse; decompose it into a spec and an ordered task list first
Keep the pre-migration static page running in a second tab to compare against the framework version feature by feature
Commit after each migrated component so a bad migration pass is isolated to one commit
Ask the assistant to name what idiom it used and why when the translation isn't obvious
Re-check accessibility and responsive behavior after migration; frameworks often lose hand-tuned CSS in translation

know_why.claim: A framework migration should be driven by a written spec, not by conversational iteration.
know_why.because: The migration touches structure across many files at once, and a wrong assumption made early (e.g. about routing) compounds into every file migrated afterward before anyone notices.
know_why.disputed_by: The vibe-loop school argues a spec written before seeing the framework's real constraints is often wrong anyway, and prefers migrating one small piece, running it, and adjusting the plan live.
know_why.source: Practitioner consensus in AI-assisted refactor writeups (Simon Willison's blog; Kent C. Dodds on incremental migration)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a 5-page static site, migrate it into a component-based framework with working client-side routing, with each page's rendered output matching the static version and no console errors.
nodes.common_failure: Asking for the whole migration in one prompt: the assistant produces a plausible-looking framework app that silently drops behavior (a form handler, a media query) buried in the original page, and the loss isn't caught because nothing was checked mid-migration.
sources: Kent C. Dodds — incremental migration writings

nodes.label: State management
nodes.one_line: Get an assistant to wire up state — local state, forms, a simple store — correctly across components instead of duplicating it per screen.
know_what: Local state — data owned by one component (useState/ref) that doesn't need to be shared, the default an AI should reach for first
Lifted state — moving state up to the nearest common parent so sibling components can share it, instead of duplicating it in each
Global store — a store (Zustand, Redux, Pinia) for state genuinely needed across distant parts of the tree, not a default reach
Derived state — a value computed from other state (a filtered list, a total) that should never itself be stored as separate state
Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs — whether a form field's value lives in component state or the DOM, and the bugs (stale value, lost input) that come from mixing the two
Stale closure — a bug class where an event handler captures an old value of state because the handler was defined before a state update, common in AI-generated effect code
know_how: Ask for the smallest-scope state first (local), and only ask for lifting or a global store when a concrete sharing need appears
Point out any state that is actually derivable from other state and ask for it to be computed instead of stored
Test every form's edge cases by hand: empty submit, rapid double-click, browser back button after a partial fill
Trace one state update through the component tree in the diff to confirm it updates every place that reads it
Ask explicitly which state is local vs shared before accepting a global store recommendation from the assistant
habits: Default to asking for local state; treat every request for global state as something to justify, not assume
Read state-update code for stale-closure risk whenever an effect or callback references a value from an outer scope
Manually exercise every branch of a form (valid, invalid, empty) after any AI change to its state logic
Keep one state 'owner' per value; flag a diff that lets two components independently mutate the same data
Re-test browser back/forward after any change to form or navigation state
nodes.checkpoint: Given a multi-step form (3 fields, one derived total, one validation error state), implement it with state that has no duplication, no stale-closure bugs, and correct behavior on browser back/forward.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting an AI's default of a global store for state that's only ever read by one component — the store then quietly becomes the place every future feature's state gets dumped, because the AI, and then the developer, follow the established pattern.
sources: Kent C. Dodds — Application State Management

nodes.label: API integration (client)
nodes.one_line: Wire a frontend to a real API client with AI assistance, handling loading and error states, not just the happy path.
know_what: Loading state — the UI state shown between request and response, which an AI-generated happy-path fetch will omit unless asked
Error state — the UI state for a failed request (4xx, 5xx, network failure), distinct from loading and distinct from empty-result
Race condition on fast navigation — a slow response for a previous request overwriting a newer one's result, a real bug in naive fetch-in-effect code
Client-side data fetching library — React Query/TanStack Query or SWR, which handles caching, retries, and race conditions that hand-rolled fetch code usually gets wrong
Optimistic update — updating the UI before the server confirms, with a rollback path if the request fails, a pattern an AI won't add unless told the UX requires it
CORS — the browser policy that blocks a client from calling an API on a different origin unless the server allows it, a common first integration failure
Request cancellation — aborting an in-flight request when the component unmounts or the input changes again, missing by default in generated fetch code
know_how: Ask explicitly for loading, error, and empty states, not just the success-path rendering
Test the integration with the network tab throttled and with the backend stopped, not only with a fast local response
Prefer a data-fetching library over hand-rolled fetch+useEffect once more than one endpoint is involved, and say so in the prompt
Check that a fast double-navigation doesn't render a stale response over a newer one
Confirm the client sends and reads the exact error shape the backend's error-handling contract defines
habits: Open the network tab on every integration change, not just the console
Simulate a failed request (kill the server, throttle to offline) before calling an integration done
Ask whether the assistant used a fetching library's cache correctly when a value doesn't update after a mutation
Treat 'it works when I click it once' as insufficient; test rapid repeated actions
Re-check CORS and error handling every time the API base URL changes (local vs deployed)
nodes.checkpoint: Given a REST endpoint, wire the frontend to it with correct loading, error, and empty states, verified by throttling the network and by stopping the backend mid-session.
nodes.common_failure: Shipping an integration that only handles the success path — the AI's first draft fetches and renders data with no loading spinner and no error boundary, and it looks done because the demo, run against a fast local backend, never hits the failure cases.

nodes.label: Full-stack deploy
nodes.one_line: Deploy a full-stack app — frontend, backend, database — with every piece correctly wired to the others in production.
know_what: Deploy target split — frontend on a static/edge host (Vercel, Netlify), backend on a server/container host (Railway, Fly.io, Render), or both together on one platform
Build-time vs runtime environment variables — a frontend value baked in at build (exposed to the client) versus a backend value read at runtime (kept server-side)
Database connection pooling — the limit on concurrent connections a serverless backend can exhaust quickly without a pooler (e.g. PgBouncer, a managed pool)
Preview deployments — a unique URL per branch/PR that exercises the real deploy pipeline before merging, catching integration breaks CI alone won't
CORS/allowed-origins config — the production frontend's real domain must be explicitly allowed on the backend, distinct from the permissive localhost setup used in development
Cold start — the latency spike on a serverless backend's first request after idling, which a frontend's loading state must tolerate
Zero-downtime deploy — a release strategy (rolling, blue-green) that avoids serving a half-updated app to a user mid-deploy
know_how: Deploy the backend and confirm it responds correctly with curl before pointing the frontend at it
Set every environment variable in the hosting platform's dashboard or CLI, never commit a working .env to the repo
Run the full user flow (load, log in, submit data, reload) against the deployed URLs, not just against localhost
Confirm the database migration ran in the deployed environment, not just locally, before considering the deploy complete
Check the browser console and network tab on the live URL for CORS or mixed-content errors
Roll the deploy back immediately if the smoke test fails, rather than debugging live in production
habits: Never treat 'it built successfully' as 'it deployed correctly' — build success and runtime correctness are different claims
Smoke-test the deployed app end to end before telling anyone it's live
Keep a written list of every environment variable each service needs, checked before each deploy
Watch the first few minutes of logs after a deploy instead of walking away once the build finishes
Re-verify CORS and allowed-origins every time a new frontend domain (staging, preview) is added
nodes.checkpoint: Deploy a frontend and backend with a shared database to production hosts, with a live end-to-end user flow (load, authenticate, create a record, see it persist on reload) working with no console errors.
nodes.common_failure: Deploying frontend and backend separately, confirming each 'works' in isolation (the frontend renders, the backend responds to curl), and skipping the one test that would have caught it — the two talking to each other with the production URLs and CORS config, not the ones used in local development.

nodes.label: Full-stack integration review
nodes.one_line: Review a full-stack app end to end — frontend, backend, data, deploy — as one coherent system before calling it production-ready.
know_what: System-level review — checking the app as one thing a user experiences, not as a checklist of components that each individually passed review
Trust boundary — every point where client input reaches the backend or database, which must be validated and authorized regardless of what the frontend enforces
End-to-end test — a test that drives the real UI against the real backend and database (Playwright, Cypress), the only check that catches an integration gap unit tests miss
Single point of failure — a dependency (one database, one external API) with no fallback, whose outage takes down the whole app
Data lifecycle review — confirming create, read, update, and delete all have working, authorized paths, not just the create flow that got demoed
Definition of production-ready — a named, specific bar (auth works, errors are handled, secrets aren't exposed, rollback exists) rather than a feeling that the app 'seems solid'
know_how: Walk every trust boundary in the app and confirm the backend, not just the frontend, enforces validation and authorization at each one
Run an end-to-end test suite against a staging environment that mirrors production, not just against localhost
Check that every CRUD path a user can reach has been exercised, not only the one shown in the last demo
Review the deployed app's logs and error tracker for anything that fired during the review session
Confirm a rollback path exists and has actually been exercised once, not just documented
Name the specific bar for 'production-ready' before the review starts, so the review has something concrete to check against
habits: Review the system as a user would encounter it — click through the real flows on the real deployed URL
Treat a passing component-level checklist as necessary but not sufficient for the system-level review
Check auth and authorization at every boundary personally, rather than trusting that each endpoint 'probably' checked it
Keep the review's findings as a concrete list (fixed / accepted risk / blocking) rather than a verbal 'looks good'
Re-run the review after any post-review fix, instead of trusting the fix in isolation

know_why.claim: The final review should be run by a human clicking through the real app, not delegated to an agent's own test summary.
know_why.because: An agent's self-report of 'all tests pass' reflects the tests it was told to write, which share the same blind spots as the implementation; a human walking the real flows catches the gap between what was specified and what a user actually needs.
know_why.disputed_by: The agentic-autonomy school argues a sufficiently broad automated suite (unit, integration, and end-to-end) plus monitoring after deploy is a better use of time than a manual click-through, and that manual review doesn't scale past the first few releases.
know_why.source: Practitioner debate on AI-assisted release practices (Simon Willison; Gergely Orosz's engineering newsletter on shipping AI-written code)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a deployed full-stack app, produce a review that walks every CRUD path and trust boundary, confirms monitoring and rollback exist, and ends in an explicit ship/no-ship decision with named blockers if any.
nodes.common_failure: Declaring the app production-ready because every individual PR passed its own review — the failure mode lives in the gaps between components (an endpoint that's secure alone but exposed once combined with a frontend route that skips a permission check), which no single component-level review would catch.
sources: Gergely Orosz — The Pragmatic Engineer newsletter
